text.p: United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union recessed negotiations on Friday after meeting throughout the day in an effort to avert a strike at the huge package carrier.
Company officials and federal mediators said they expected the talks to resume soon, but gave no set time.
"The talks are in recess. They are subject to recall by federal mediators," UPS spokeswoman Gina Ellrich said.
Ellrich told reporters there had been no indication that any kind of job action was imminent and mediators said they expected the negotiations to resume.
"I certainly don't consider it a breakdown," director of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service John Calhoun Wells said.
Earlier on Friday, Teamsters President Ron Carey threatened a walkout if contract issuues were not resolved.
"If we fail to find some solution ... then we will be on strike," Carey said as negotiations began.
The two sides resumed talks on Friday afternoon after the International Brotherhood of Teamsters let a midnight strike deadline pass without taking any action.
After the two sides had been meeting for several hours on Friday, David Helfert, a spokesman for the federal mediation service, said negotiations would continue into the evening.
The negotiations cover a range of issues, the union said, including the creation of more full-time jobs, an end to subcontracting, and safety, health and pension issues.

A strike against the company could throw the country's package delivery service into chaos, stranding more than 12 million parcels destined for about 1.5 million U.S. customers a day. It would also put about 200,000 Teamsters out of work.
UPS said the strike threat had caused it to lose out on a substantial quantity of its delivery business and that it had already had to temporarily lay off hundreds of full- and part-time workers.
"UPS has had to lay off some of its workers," Ellrich said.

"It's an exaggerated scare tactic on their part," said Teamster spokesman Rand Wilson of UPS reports about declining company business. But he did concede it was a problem, adding that the company had brought it upon itself by dragging its feet in negotiations. "We warned them: don't bring it down to the wire," he said.

The Teamsters also issued a statement saying the London-based International Transport Workers Federation stands ready to activate a worldwide campaign in solidarity with UPS workers if a strike occurs.
Meanwhile, drug companies said a UPS strike could pose a threat to the delivery of drugs and medical supplies to hospitals and eventually could affect critically ill patients.

"It's a major concern for us because it affects how we are going to get our medications to the people who need them, particularly critically ill patients," said Amy Magan, a spokesman for pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly and Co.

UPS is the largest package carrier in the country with 1996 revenues of $22.4 billion. It handles 3.15 billion parcels and documents shipped annually to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
